s09.slug: FRIDAY · 10:05 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: The Fishbowl has gone orange. Theo has put orange party bulbs in both lamps, and the glass walls give the room back to itself over the black water of the Lagoon. Between episodes his MacBook, cabled into the TV in the corner, plays “TiK ToK” at a volume Priya has twice called a choice.
On the door at eye level hangs a placard, laminated, in Comic Sans: THE SITUATION ROOM. Priya came down at ten to see about the noise, read it, and asked the room, “Who laminated this.”
“A citizen,” said Theo, and she left with a fistful of Cheetos and her mouth set.

The Cheetos are in a cut-glass punch bowl with a ladle. Beside the bowl, on the coffee table, stands a bottle of spray tan, unopened, which Theo has declined to explain. *Jersey Shore* premiered last night, and Theo has it again tonight through the cable — eight strangers moving into a house in Seaside Heights and introducing themselves to the camera by their nicknames, and one of them by his stomach muscles — and he loves it with a sincerity Jack finds frightening. “Picture it,” he told them at ten, on his feet in a cashmere V-neck with nothing under it. “Eight people. One house. No adult supervision. It’s *Amarcord* with a tanning bed.”

Laney dances on the arm of the couch in a Pi Lam tank top whenever the music comes up and sits on it when the show comes back. When the little one with the hair arrives with her suitcase and announces herself to the house, Laney points the remote at her like a scepter. “Y’all. That’s *me*. That’s me without a sponsor.” Margot has the armchair; she has told them twice she’s here for anthropology. “It’s a kinship structure,” she says, of the man with the stomach muscles explaining what he calls himself. “Lévi-Strauss with hair gel.” Kevin has orgo flashcards on his knee that he hasn’t turned over since the hot tub. “I want that man’s bloodwork,” he says. Doug Pruitt, in his Tauren-druid hoodie, says “Duuuude” at the stomach muscles with every one of its vowels.

Lena is on the couch with her boots off and her feet tucked under her and her head on Julian’s shoulder. Julian watches the show the way he watches everything, carefully, in case it turns out to be in a key. Theo served him his Cheetos last, in a paper cup, and called him Mr. Park-Ellis both times. When a girl on the screen cries on a boardwalk in the dark, Lena says without lifting her head, “Somebody’s mama in New Jersey is lighting a candle right now,” and Julian laughs, low, and Jack looks back at the TV.
At 11:52 the RAZR goes against his thigh. He reads it with the screen turned in to his chest.

body.text: early. marine lab turnout. im bored of being early

body: At 11:55 he stands up.
Laney stops dancing on the couch arm. “Where are you *going*?” She points at the screen with her whole arm. “It’s *Snooki*.”
The phone goes again in his hand.
“Who’s *that*?”
“No one.”

response: “Bed.”
“Bed’s *upstairs*, fireman,” Laney says. “That’s the front door.”
Lena lifts her head off Julian’s shoulder and watches him to the door. On the screen somebody in the hot tub is shouting at somebody who isn’t.
“And there he goes,” Theo says, with his eyes on the hot tub.
“I have a situation.”
Theo puts a hand over his heart, betrayed and proud in about equal parts. “He’s *learning*.”
Lena lifts her head off Julian’s shoulder and watches him to the door. On the screen somebody in the hot tub is shouting at somebody who isn’t.
“And there he goes,” Theo says, with his eyes on the hot tub.
“Out.”
“Out *where*?”
“Just out.”
Laney’s sunglasses come down out of her hair onto her nose, slowly, and she looks at him over them until he’s past the punch bowl.
Lena lifts her head off Julian’s shoulder and watches him to the door. On the screen somebody in the hot tub is shouting at somebody who isn’t.
“And there he goes,” Theo says, with his eyes on the hot tub.

s12.slug: SATURDAY · 3:38 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAWN
body: He hears it from the Lagoon path: the Delgado alarm, the same goose-honk it has made at three in the morning since August, coming to him across the black water a quarter mile out. She dropped him at the Marine Lab turnout at 3:33 with the engine running and her flannel still inside out and was gone before he had the door shut. He runs. The path is dark under the eucalyptus and loud with his own boots, and the cold comes in through the open shirt. He buttons the shirt while he runs and gets it wrong by one hole, top to bottom.

He comes onto the lawn from the wrong side — up from the water, out of the eucalyptus, not out of the door — past Rafi Ochoa sitting on the curb of the path in a hooded surf poncho, who watches him come up out of the trees at a dead run and says, approvingly, “Boss.” And into the tail of Alarm Five: three hundred people in towels and comforters and somebody’s sleeping bag on the wet grass under the trees, the horn still going, a Marisol Fire engine idling on Anacapa Way with its lights turning over all of them because this is the fifth time, and the moon up over the lawn like it bought a ticket.

Priya is in the middle of it with the laminated roster on a clipboard and a headlamp on her forehead. On the back of the clipboard, facing the crowd, a second laminate: FIFTH TIME. I KNOW. Every name on four has a check by it but one. A firefighter in a turnout coat leans down to ask her if everybody’s out, and Priya tells him everybody but one, and that the one is being *accounted for*, in a voice that makes him straighten up and go back to the engine.

Theo stands in front of her in the navy silk robe with the gray camera bag and the black bag both on his shoulder, mid-sentence. “— a condition, very Catholic, they do it in silence, it’s a whole tradition, there are *orders* of it —” He sees Jack over her head, coming up out of the trees, and doesn’t miss a syllable. “And there he is. Out of the shower.”
Priya turns. The headlamp turns with her and gets him full in the face.
“Costigan.” She lowers the clipboard. “You were not on my lawn.” The headlamp goes down him and comes back up. “You’re *dry*.”

Lena is sitting on the grass beside Laney under Laney’s pink comforter, with the quilt off her own bed around her shoulders. She’s looking at the strip of empty grass beside Theo, about the width of a person. Then she looks at him, coming up from the water at 3:38 in last night’s clothes, with his shirt done up wrong and the moon on him. She has nothing to say about it.
Laney has plenty. “Fireman,” she says. “You’re *dressed*.”

Kevin is running the other half of the roll with his own clipboard, in the navy quarter-zip and plaid pajama pants. Beside COSTIGAN, in pencil, Jack can see from here, there’s a small neat question mark. Down at the far end of the building Doug Pruitt stands barefoot in the wet grass with his pillow under his arm, blinking at the fire engine.
His shirt is wrong from the collar down, and he can still feel exactly where her hand was under it.

journal.title: The 3 a.m. alarm
journal.text: Alarm 1, Monday the 31st, 3:07: everybody on the lawn in what they sleep in; Theo saved the espresso machine; Margot wrote ‘ALARM 1’ like it was a case number. Alarm 2, Friday the 18th, 3:12: eighteen days. Margot says that’s not a schedule, it’s a person. She’s keeping a log. Tuesday the 6th, nothing. Either the theory’s wrong or he’s on vacation. Alarm 3, Tuesday the 13th, 3:20, in a storm, under the overhang: twenty-five days. Margot says he’s irregular or he’s two people. Alarm 4, Sunday the 8th, 3:11: twenty-six days. Margot staked out the lounge pull station all night with Theo’s camera and Gold Bond on the handle. She fell asleep at 2:50 for the first time in recorded history. It came from the east stair. Alarm 5, Saturday the 5th, 3:10. Twenty-seven days. Margot said twenty-six. I wasn’t on the lawn. I came up from the water at 3:38. Theo told Priya I was in the shower.

response: “Shower,” Jack says.
Priya looks at his legs. “You’re wearing *jeans*.”
“He’s very modest,” says Theo.
Priya writes something on the roster that takes longer than a check mark. Over on Kevin’s clipboard the question mark is still there in pencil when Kevin turns the page.

The horn cuts out in the middle of a honk, and three hundred people say *finally* at once and start back for the doors with their bedding. Margot comes by him on her way to the stairs, in a black peacoat over black pajamas, the Moleskine in her pocket and her hands with it.

“Alarm Five,” she says. “Three-ten. Twenty-seven days. I said twenty-six.” She doesn’t slow down, and she drops her voice for the rest of it. “Out past one, four nights of six. Three-oh-five looks down on the front walk, Costigan, and I don’t sleep. I count.” A step on, without turning around: “I’m not writing it down.”

He goes up the east stairs with the ranch road’s dust still on his boots. In 412 the gray bag and the black one are back on the top shelf of Theo’s closet, and Theo is in bed in the robe, turned to the wall. Jack sits on his own bed and gets one boot off.
Theo doesn’t turn over. “You’re welcome.”

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. It was still there when I went in.

s13.slug: SATURDAY · 2:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: The basement laundry room smells the way it always does on a Saturday afternoon, sweet and chemical, warm lint and somebody’s dryer sheets, and Jack comes down the stairs into it with a pillowcase full of everything that smells like surf wax and somebody’s dog.
Theo is sitting on a dryer.

Theo sends his laundry out to a woman in town who irons his T-shirts. He has never used a dryer in this building. He is sitting on top of Dryer 3, under Priya’s laminated sign about the quarters, in his loafers, with his ankles crossed. Laney is cross-legged on the folding table with a legal pad on her knee and her sunglasses on, indoors, in a basement. Their heads are together over the pad.
They come apart.
“We were discussing —” Laney says, “— finals.”
At the same moment, Theo: “The situation.”

Laney turns the legal pad over on her knee. On its cardboard back, in Sharpie: PROPERTY OF PI LAMBDA CHI — DO NOT REMOVE FROM HOUSE. On the dryer at Theo’s hip there’s a box of laundry soap with the price tag still on it.

They don’t leave. Jack takes the washer at the end of the row, and the two of them give their attention to the ceiling — the pipes, the sprinkler heads, a water stain over the door that Theo regards with real interest. Jack upends the pillowcase into the machine: the flannel, the jeans, the shirt he buttoned wrong.

“It’s a study group,” Theo offers. “For finals. We meet down here for the acoustics. Laney has a theory about the dryers — the white noise, the warmth, it’s very good for retention, they did a study at Stanford, or one of the Stanfords. Every Saturday. Two-thirty. Very exclusive.” He re-crosses his ankles. “You’d hate it.”
Laney doesn’t look at Theo while he says any of it. She’s watching the shirt go into the machine. “Jack,” she says. “Separate your darks.”

response: “Finals,” Jack says. “In the laundry room.”
Theo indicates the room — the dryers, the folding table, the sign about the quarters — with one open hand. “It’s a situation room.”
Laney nods at that, as if it settles it, and goes on looking at the pipes.
He picks the darks back out without a word and puts them in the next machine over, and feeds both of them quarters.
Laney leans over to Theo, low, not low enough. “He *separates*.”

choices.text: “If you want to know where I was, ask.”
response: “If you want to know where I was,” Jack says, “ask.”
Laney looks at him over the legal pad. “We don’t want to *know*, Jack. We want to *guess*.”
Theo says nothing at all.

s14.slug: SATURDAY · 3:35 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSION LINE
body: At half past three the sun is low enough to come in through the blue glass sideways, and it throws the windows across the side aisle in long blue panes, one to a pew. The confession line waits in them on folding chairs, under the ribs of the hull, six people facing the old coat closet and its card in Mrs. Fitch’s capitals: KNOCK (gently). Mrs. Fitch has the card table by the door, a tin of lemon bars, and her ears open.
Jack has the chair nearest the closet. Joey Abruzzo has the one behind him.
“*Jack!*” Joey leans forward to his ear at full Staten Island volume. “Big one?”
“*Joseph*,” says Mrs. Fitch, from the door, without looking up.
“Sorry, Mrs. Fitch,” Joey whispers, at the same volume.
The closet door opens, and a girl from the choir comes out with her face scrubbed and goes up the aisle to the votive rack. It’s his turn.

choices.key: Saturday you went into the box and told Fr. Osei about a girl.
Saturday you stepped out of the confession line.

s14a.slug: SATURDAY · 3:50 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSIONAL
body: The coat closet is the size it has always been: a kneeler on this side, a folding chair on the other, and in the middle the linen screen on its wooden frame, with a shape behind it in a purple stole. The coat hooks are still on the back wall from 1962, and somebody has thumbtacked a holy card of the Prodigal Son to the inside of the door at eye level, where only the penitents see it. Jack kneels. On the far side of the linen the chair creaks, and the bad leg finds its place, and Osei settles and waits for him with all the time in the world.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned.”

body.text: “It’s been two and a half weeks since my last confession.” The last penance is done; he finished it at the first candle, in Youngstown.

body: He has the next part ready, and it still comes out in pieces. “There’s a girl,” he says. “Not the one I —” He stops. “A girl.”
The shape behind the linen waits.

“I keep putting myself where I know what’s going to happen,” Jack says. “In her car. Two in the morning. Up the coast somewhere, where nobody knows where I am.” His knees hurt already. “I don’t stop it. Monday it was her phone that stopped it — an alarm she set so she’d leave. I didn’t set one.” Outside the door, faintly, Joey Abruzzo is explaining something to somebody about the Yankees. “And then I go again.”

body.text: “Last night,” he says. “I was the one who slowed it down. I don’t know if that counts.”
“Last night I told her what I want,” he says. “Out loud. I meant it.”

body: “And the rest of the week.” He leaves it there, without a list, and Osei leaves it with him.
On the other side of the linen a long breath goes out.
“I was a doctor before I was this,” Osei says, “and a doctor asks the dull question first, because it is the one that tells him where it hurts. Do you want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens?”

response: “Stop what happens,” Jack says. “Not her.”

“Then change the hour.” Osei says it like a prescription, something to take with food. “The near occasion is rarely the person, my friend. It is two in the morning, and a car, and nobody who knows where you are. Bring her into the daylight.” A pause, and the chair. “If she won’t come into the daylight, that is also an answer.”
“Wanting her is not the sin. You know that, or you would not be so tired.” A breath. “For your penance,” Osei says, “a decade of the rosary for her. Not about her. For her. By her name.”
Jack says the Act of Contrition, the one he learned in second grade at St. Brigid’s, fast at the start and slower where it counts, and through the linen the shape lifts its hand.

“God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“The Lord has freed you from your sins. Go in peace.”
He came in carrying it, and he’s kneeling in the back pew under the last of the blue light without it. He can’t account for that. He never can. It’s true anyway.
He prays the decade on his knuckles: ten Hail Marys, and her name at the top of every one. *Skye.*

response.text: It’s the second time he has said it to God. The first was at St. Brigid’s, at the first candle, with Nonna at the end of the pew.
response.else: It’s the first time he has said it to God.

response: Up front, Joey Abruzzo gets to his feet and knocks on the closet door, three times, gently, as the card says.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Bring her into the daylight.

response: “I don’t know,” Jack says.

s14b.slug: SATURDAY · 3:40 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE DOOR
body: He gets up off the folding chair. Behind him Joey Abruzzo’s eyebrows go up.
“Go ahead, Joey.”
Joey goes ahead at speed, and Jack hears him knock anyway, gently, on the open door.
At the card table by the door Mrs. Fitch doesn’t look up from her crossword. “Not today, Mr. Costigan?”
“Not today.”

“Father’s here till a quarter to five,” she says, filling in a word. “And next Saturday. And the one after. He’s very reliable. It’s one of his only faults.” She takes the lid off the tin anyway and holds it out to him, the way she would to anybody, and he takes a lemon bar. Outside, the A-frame’s courtyard is bright enough to make him squint after the blue, and he has a shift at seven and four hours to fill before it. He sits on the steps with the lemon bar and watches the broken sprinkler in the courtyard work at the olive tree, a click at a time, missing it every time.
